Press Release:


Honeymoon Murder Trial Week 7
Shrien Dewani faces either acquittal or the witness stand. Carte Blanche analyses the seventh week of the Honeymoon Murder trial, a week in which the State closed its case and Dewani’s lawyers applied to the Western Cape High Court for their client’s acquittal on charges of conspiring to have his new wife Anni Dewani killed.


Script:


DEWANI WEEK SEVEN TRIAL

John Webb:
Seven weeks ago, Cape Town braced for the long-awaited Honeymoon Murder Trial. It had taken South African authorities close to four years to successfully extradite murder-accused Shrien Dewani. He was charged with orchestrating the kidnapping and murder of his newly wed wife, Anni. There was intrigue right from the start when Dewani in his plea explanation admitted to being bisexual. Several State witnesses tried to evade the cameras. Judge Traverso deemed certain evidence inadmissible and showed irritation toward the State at times. Dramatic CCTV footage was shown, and a day was spent commemorating the fourth anniversary of Anni’s death. On everybody’s lips- did Dewani orchestrate the murder of his wife or were the four co-conspirators acting alone?

The State closed its case on Monday and Defense Advocate Francois Van Zyl immediately said that he would be applying for a discharge under Section 174 of the Criminal Procedures Act.

The families left the court quietly. The Defense went to start working on their arguments, which had to be handed in on Wednesday. The State’s response was to be handed in on Friday.

David O’Sullivan:
Cliffy, what exactly is a Section 174 application?

Cliff Alexander:
David, section 174 of the Criminal Procedures Act 51 of 1977 reads as follows, “If at the close of the case for the prosecution at any trial, the Court is of the opinion, that is important, the Court is of the opinion that there is no evidence that the accused committed the offense referred to in the chart sheet or any offense of which he may be convicted on the charge, it may, important again, may return a verdict of ‘not guilty.’

David O’Sullivan:
In other words, the judge may say, ‘There is no case for Shrien Dewani to answer. You can go free, you are not guilty.’

Annelene Van Den Heever:
Indeed, what the Judge will have to do though, she will have to very carefully look at the evidence that was presented, and we must remember that the evidence is not only the direct evidence that was presented, i.e. witnesses’ testimony, but it’s also circumstantial evidence that she can take into the equation and make a decision on.

John Webb:
Defense Attorney Cliff Alexander and Defense Advocate Annelene Van Den Heever have been following the case closely. They understand the importance of Judge Traverso’s decision and the repercussions that could follow for Shrien Dewani, especially if he has to take the stand in his own defense.

David O’Sullivan:
So by putting Shrien Dewani on the stand, under cross-examination, he may incriminate himself-

Cliff Alexander:
Correct!

David O’Sullivan:
- and that is in breach of our Constitution and his right to a fair trial.

Cliff Alexander:
Let’s say that he has to testify and is convicted based on self-incriminating evidence he gives, it could be argued that later that had she granted, and she should have granted, the 174 application, he wouldn’t have had to testify, he wouldn’t have incriminated himself. He’s got a right not to incriminate himself.

John Webb:
So Court 2 was empty this week as the legal teams buckled down ahead of a vital moment in the trial.

At this crucial point in the trial, let’s reflect back on the State’s case and how their witnesses performed under cross-examination.

The first bombshell of the trial was when Dewani, in his plea explanation, said he was bisexual and had sexual relationships with male prostitutes.

Andrew Plant:
A pre-emptive strike they’re calling it in the papers back in the UK, for example if there was going to be some sort of sensational revelation by the prosecution here about Shrien Dewani’s sexuality, perhaps saying that he was gay, maybe establishing a motive for him being unhappy in his relationship with Anni Dewani. Well what they’ve done here is seemingly open and honest.

John Webb:
The State tried using various witnesses to provide a motive as to why Dewani wanted his wife killed. According to them, his conflicted sexuality.

Simon Johnson, IT specialist, testified that Dewani had visited a gay site two days after Anni’s body was found.

It’s clear that the State wanted to use Shrien Dewani’s sexuality as one of the cornerstones of its case, but Judge Traverso ruled that that evidence was irrelevant and therefore inadmissible.

And that included detailed evidence from the German so-called bondage master, who only made a brief appearance in the witness box.

Nicholas Parker, a journalist with The Sun newspaper in the United Kingdom was called to the stand. He gave testimony about an interview that he conducted with Shrien Dewani shortly after Anni’s murder.
In that interview, he said, Shrien made no reference to the infamous helicopter ride he said he had planned for his wife. That however is in his plea explanation. Zola Tongo testified that the R10,000 left in the hijacked car was payment for the crime. Dewani says that money was left there for him to pay for the helicopter trip. Advocate Van Den Heever says that this is suspicious. Why? Because he didn’t mention the R10,000 to the police when questioned after the crime.

Annelene Van Den Heever:
Now the question arises, why would you not tell the police, ‘Listen, part of the loot that the robbers got away with was R10, 000.’? He made mention of phones, a purse, jewelry, but you leave out the very important factor of the R10,000. So it’s all these other circumstantial evidence that the court of course can take into account when making the decision.

John Webb:
Sneha Mashru, Anni’s cousin and closest confidant, came to the stand. She provided emotional testimony, including how she found Shrien’s behavior after Anni’s killing to be quite suspicious.

William Booth:
Well again, it’s only a perception, and she’s certainly not an expert that can come to court and tell the court, ‘Look, because somebody has reacted in a certain way, you can draw inferences from that.’

John Webb:
Advocate Van Zyl complained that some of Sneha Mashru’s evidence was hearsay. For example, she said that Anni had confided to her before coming to South Africa, she was thinking of getting a divorce. Judge Traverso agreed, saying, ‘I am not going to allow an atmosphere to be created in this court by inadmissible evidence.’

The State called police ballistics expert Peter Engelbrecht to the stand. He provided testimony on the position of the shooter inside the vehicle when Anni was killed, but his evidence was torn to shreds.

He was forced to concede that the evidence he gave in the trial of Xolile Mgeni, who was convicted for being the triggerman and who got life for Anni’s murder, may have misled the court. He admitted that he had taken no measurements to support his theory. He also admitted that he had only taken measurements very recently in this trial, and that he had used a different model car with different seating configurations. The three co-conspirators who took to the stand faced grueling cross-examination. Tongo was in the box for a total of seven days. It was put to Mziwamadoda Qwabe, who struck a plea bargain with the State, that he was actually the shooter, not Mgeni, especially because gun residue was found on one of the gloves he wore on that night. Monde Mbolombo, the so-called middleman who was not prosecuted for his role, came to the stand and admitted that he had lied in his original police statement, his 204 statement, and the trial of Mgeni. This time he was going to tell the truth.

Advocate Van Zyl confronted Tongo time and again as to why the evidence he told this court is different to or not included in his original police statement. Tongo explained these inconsistencies by saying, ‘As time goes on, I can just remember some of the things. Some of the things are resurfacing.’

Cliff Alexander:
There are certain parts of his evidence that will stand, there is no doubt about that, but I think that the material contradictions are going to count against him. And as Anne has said, he is the only person who could actually finger Dewani.

David O’Sullivan:
Were there sufficient building blocks to establish the State’s case through Tongo’s evidence?

Annelene Van Den Heever:
Again, I believe if you look at the case, at the credibility of a witness, the mere fact that a witness lies, the mere fact that he admits that he lied, doesn’t attract, at the end of the day, from the fact as to whether you can believe his evidence or not. I don’t think he was a good witness, but I do not think his evidence was so bad that the court at this stage, taking into account the circumstantial evidence, can dismiss it out of hand and say, ‘Well, he was a poor witness; the quality of his evidence was so poor that I don’t need to put Dewani on his defense.’

David O’Sullivan:
What are your thoughts on this, Cliffy?

Cliff Alexander:
There is one issue we’ve got to keep in mind. Colonel Hendrickse, when he testified, conceded that he had possibly conveyed to an attorney during his interrogation of the accomplices per se, some of the gentlemen who testified, they conveyed to him that they never intended to murder, to shoot Anni Dewani. They shot her because she wouldn’t stop screaming.

John Webb:
Captain Paul Hendrickse of the Hawks, who also took the stand, was the principal investigator.

Cliff Alexander:
If there was a conspiracy to commit murder, one would’ve assumed that they would’ve said, ‘We intended to kill her, to murder her,’ but that seen in isolation and then measured up with Tongo’s evidence per se, where there was this alleged conspiracy where he was approached by Mr. Dewani to arrange the so-called hit. It doesn’t make sense, it doesn’t add up.

John Webb:
So, a big decision for Judge Traverso. She will also need to apply her mind to all the CCTV footage which some feel showed Dewani acting suspiciously. Expect a packed gallery tomorrow and an extra contingent of international news crews to hear the decision.

David O’Sullivan:
How do you think the judge is going to rule on this matter?

Annelene Van Den Heever:
I do not believe she’s going to give him a discharge.

David O’Sullivan:
Cliffy?

Cliff Alexander:
To quote the famous Judge Claasen, I believe she’ll say to the State, ‘You fail to prove a prima facie case against the accused. You cannot now seek the accused’s assistance to do what you cannot do.’
